blocks.text: Have you ever wondered why the order in which you access elements in an array can drastically affect the performance of your program? This is due to how data is stored and accessed in memory, and understanding this can help you write more efficient code.

blocks.markdown: In computer systems, memory hierarchy plays a crucial role in determining the performance of programs. The hierarchy consists of various levels of memory storage, from fast and small caches to slower and larger main memory and disk storage. Accessing data efficiently from these storage levels can significantly impact the speed of your program.

blocks.title: Cache
blocks.text: A cache is a smaller, faster memory located closer to the CPU, which stores copies of frequently accessed data from main memory to speed up data retrieval.

blocks.markdown: When you access data in a program, the CPU first checks whether the data is in the cache. If it is, this is called a cache hit, and the data is retrieved quickly. If not, it results in a cache miss, and the data must be fetched from slower memory, which takes more time.

blocks.latex: EAT = (1 - \text{miss rate}) \times \text{cache access time} + \text{miss rate} \times \text{miss penalty}
blocks.caption: Effective Access Time (EAT) formula

blocks.markdown: The Effective Access Time (EAT) is a measure of the average time required to access data, factoring in both cache hits and misses. Minimizing cache misses is crucial for optimizing performance.

blocks.title: Row-Major vs Column-Major Traversal
blocks.prompt: Consider a 2D array stored in row-major order. Compare the performance of row-major and column-major traversals.

steps.text: 1. In row-major order, consecutive elements of a row are stored contiguously in memory.
2. Accessing elements in row-major order results in fewer cache misses because adjacent elements are likely to be in the same cache line.
3. In column-major traversal, elements in different rows are accessed consecutively, leading to more cache misses as these elements are not stored contiguously.

blocks.answer: Row-major traversal is more cache-friendly because it accesses contiguous memory locations, reducing cache misses.

blocks.title: Locality of Reference
blocks.text: Programs with good locality of reference access data in a way that takes advantage of the cache, leading to fewer cache misses and improved performance.

blocks.title: Estimating Cache Miss Impact

blocks.markdown: Understanding how memory access patterns affect cache performance is vital for writing efficient code. By optimizing data access patterns, you can significantly reduce cache misses and improve the running time of your programs.
